literal: In serving his widowed sister-in-law he was most careful; in raising the orphan son Shu, his kindness and acceptance ran especially deep.
idiomatic: He cared for his widowed sister-in-law with scrupulous devotion and raised the orphan Shu with an affection that ran unusually deep.

literal: While in Yan province, when a capital messenger reported that Shu was ill, he at once grew anxious, abandoned sleep and food, and his complexion faded.
idiomatic: While stationed in Yan province, he heard from a capital courier that Shu had fallen ill and was seized with worry at once—he stopped eating and sleeping, and his face grew haggard.

literal: When Shu died, men of standing grieved with him; though his mourning ran very deep, he never cried again—when guests came to console him, he only wiped away tears.
idiomatic: When Shu died, scholars and officials mourned with him. His grief ran deep, yet he would not weep again; when guests came to condole, he merely dabbed at his eyes.

literal: His lofty feeling and penetrating insight in dispelling stagnant burdens—since Dongmen Wu, there has been nothing like it.
idiomatic: In lofty feeling and far-seeing insight, in lifting burdens that weigh on the heart, no one since Dongmen Wu had done the like.

literal: He had collected works in thirty scrolls, circulating in the world.
idiomatic: His collected writings ran to thirty scrolls and circulated widely.

literal: His son Dabao had literary feeling.
idiomatic: His son Xing Dabao had a gift for letters.

literal: Illegitimate sons Dade and Dadao scarcely knew characters at all.
idiomatic: His illegitimate sons Dade and Dadao could barely read.

literal: The full text uses the Zhonghua Shuju first edition of the Book of Northern Qi (November 1972) as the base for collation.
idiomatic: The full text uses the Zhonghua Shuju first edition of the Book of Northern Qi (November 1972) as the base for collation.
